outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the survey's scope, covering the evolution of LLM security from 2023 to 2026. It highlights the transition from simple prompt-based exploits to sophisticated architectural vulnerabilities, including data poisoning, adversarial attacks, hallucinations, and prompt injection. The abstract summarizes key findings regarding the fragility of safety alignment (RLHF/DPO) and the emerging threats in autonomous agentic systems and reasoning models (LRMs).

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: This section motivates the need for a comprehensive security analysis of Large Language Models (LLMs) as they transition from chatbots to autonomous agents. It outlines the rapid evolution of the research landscape between 2023 and 2026, noting the shift from manual red-teaming to automated, multi-modal, and reasoning-aware attacks. The introduction defines the scope of the survey, encompassing training-time interventions (poisoning) and inference-time exploits (adversarial attacks, prompt injection), while also addressing the reliability crisis posed by hallucinations. It concludes with a summary of the paper's contributions to the academic community.

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Provides the technical foundation for understanding LLM security. It covers LLM architectural basics (Transformer, MoE), the standard training pipeline (Pre-training, SFT, RLHF, DPO), and the core concepts of safety alignment. This section establishes a formal threat model, defining attacker capabilities (white-box vs. black-box), access levels (training data vs. inference API), and objectives (integrity, availability, confidentiality). Key terminology such as Attack Success Rate (ASR), Jailbreaking, and Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) are formally defined here.

outline.title: Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities
outline.description: Analyzes how attackers manipulate the LLM supply chain and training process. It details the fragility of alignment techniques like RLHF and DPO against label-flipping and preference manipulation [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF, Kusaka_2025_LLM]. The section explores domain-specific poisoning in code generation [Yan_2024_LLM] and the cross-lingual transferability of backdoors [He_2024_LLMs]. A major focus is placed on the 2025 shift toward 'behavioral' and 'reasoning' poisoning, where Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes are hijacked to induce deceptive reasoning [Zhu_2025_Think, Shen_2025_Decepchain].

outline.title: Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaking Mechanisms
outline.description: Examines inference-time exploits designed to bypass safety guardrails. It traces the evolution from early prompt-based exploits to sophisticated white-box analysis of neuron activations [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring]. The section covers interaction-based vulnerabilities, including multi-turn conversational exploits [Hao_2024_Exploring] and 'context-shifting' in expert programming environments [Noever_2024_AI]. It also addresses the weaponization of LLM agents for autonomous CVE exploitation and the susceptibility of the ReAct framework to control-flow hijacking [Fa].

outline.title: Prompt Injection in Autonomous and Reasoning Systems
outline.description: Focuses on the specific challenges of Prompt Injection (PI) and its evolution into agentic environments. It discusses structural vulnerabilities like 'FlipAttack' and 'AutoDan' [Liu_2024_Flipattack, Liu_2024_Autodan]. A significant portion is dedicated to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in multi-modal environments, such as web navigation and coding editors [Shi_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_Webinject]. The section also analyzes the unique vulnerabilities of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) like DeepSeek-R1, where internal CoT processes provide new attack surfaces [Cui_2025_LLM, Cui_2025_LLMs].

outline.title: Hallucinations and the Integrity of LLM Outputs
outline.description: Investigates the security implications of LLM hallucinations, treating them as a threat to factual integrity. It covers the 'language prior' problem in Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) [Wang_2024_Mllm, Xing_2024_Mitigating] and the use of Natural Language Inference (NLI) for factual consistency checking [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative]. The section highlights the 2025 trend of using specialized small-scale models for hallucination detection [Ivry_2025_Paladin, Yaron_2025_GPT] and the challenges of grounding in specialized domains like healthcare and climate science [Thulke_2025_Listen, Agarwal_2].

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Synthesizes defensive research into a holistic framework. It moves from simple prompt engineering to internal activation monitoring and architectural guardrails [Cheng_2024_Unit]. The section covers pre-processing defenses (perplexity filters), in-processing methods (robust RLHF, adversarial training), and post-processing filters. It also discusses the role of specialized 'safety models' and the challenges of defending against indirect injections in autonomous agents [Shi_2025_LLM].

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation Frameworks
outline.description: A mandatory, comprehensive review of how LLM security is measured. This section synthesizes benchmarks and metrics across all categories. It covers adversarial benchmarks like AdvBench, poisoning evaluation via label-flipping ASR, and hallucination benchmarks such as those using NLI [Jing_2024_Scale]. It discusses automated red-teaming tools, evolutionary algorithms for black-box generation [Liu_2024_Autodan], and the use of 'LLM-as-a-judge' for evaluating safety. Critical metrics like ASR, perplexity-based detection rates, and faithfulness scores are compared.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Identifies critical gaps in current LLM security research. It discusses the 'cat-and-mouse' game between attackers and defenders, the limitations of current benchmarks in capturing long-term agentic risks, and the emerging threats posed by reasoning-heavy models (LRMs). This section also explores the ethical implications of red-teaming and the difficulty of ensuring safety in multilingual and multimodal contexts where data is scarce.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: Summarizes the key findings of the survey, emphasizing that LLM security is a multi-layered problem requiring defenses at the data, model, and system levels. It provides practical recommendations for developers and researchers, stressing the importance of continuous red-teaming and the development of more robust, reasoning-aware safety alignments. The conclusion reiterates the need for standardized evaluation to keep pace with the rapid evolution of LLM capabilities.
